name: Desiderius Erasmus
role: Catholic priest and humanist scholar, editor of the Greek New Testament

died.cause: Illness (dysentery), after years of poor health

summary: The most famous scholar of the Renaissance, whose printed Greek New Testament became the basis for the Reformation's Bible translations. He criticized church abuses but stayed Catholic and broke publicly with Luther, so he was attacked from both sides.

key_dates.label: Enters the Augustinian canons at Steyn
First visit to England; meets Thomas More and John Colet
Publishes the first edition of the Adages
Publishes the first printed Greek New Testament with a new Latin translation
Publishes On Free Will against Luther
Leaves Protestant Basel for Catholic Freiburg im Breisgau

accomplishments.text: Published the first printed edition of the Greek New Testament (1516), with a new Latin translation and notes. His later editions became the basis of the "Received Text" used by Luther, Tyndale, and the King James translators.
In his third edition (1522) added the passage 1 John 5:7–8 known as the "Johannine Comma," which he had left out of earlier editions because he did not find it in Greek manuscripts.

Wrote The Praise of Folly (1511), a satire of the corruption of clergy, monks, and theologians, and the Handbook of the Christian Soldier (Enchiridion, 1503), which called for inward, Bible-centered piety.
Edited the works of Church Fathers, including Jerome (1516), Augustine, and others, making them widely available in print.
Compiled the Adages, a growing collection of thousands of classical proverbs with commentary.
Wrote On Free Will (1524), defending human free will against Luther, who replied with The Bondage of the Will (1525). The exchange marked his public break with the Reformation.
Declined Pope Paul III's offer to make him a cardinal in 1535, citing his age and health.

popularized.phrase: "In the land of the blind, the one-eyed man is king" (In regione caecorum rex est luscus)
popularized.note: An older proverb that became widely known through his Adages.

misattributed.phrase: "When I get a little money I buy books; and if any is left I buy food and clothes."
misattributed.note: A loose modern paraphrase of a 1500 letter to his friend Jacob Batt, in which he wrote that when money came he would first buy Greek authors and then clothes.

persecution_note: Erasmus was never arrested or tried. He was attacked by conservative Catholic theologians, who accused him of preparing the way for Luther, and he lost Protestant friends after breaking with Luther. The Paris theology faculty formally censured his writings, the Spanish church investigated them, and after his death Pope Paul IV banned all his works. He also left Basel when it turned Protestant.

persecution.title: Writings censured by the Paris theology faculty
persecution.summary: The Faculty of Theology of the University of Paris (the Sorbonne), led by its syndic Noël Béda, condemned his Colloquies (1526) and later issued formal censures of many passages from his works, published in 1531.

responsible.name: Noël Béda
responsible.role: Syndic (head) of the Paris theology faculty; his chief critic

responsible.name: Faculty of Theology, University of Paris

persecution.outcome: His books were condemned in Paris, but no action was taken against him personally.

persecution.title: Investigated by Spanish theologians at Valladolid
persecution.summary: Members of Spanish religious orders accused his writings of heresy, and a conference of theologians met at Valladolid under the Inquisitor General, Alonso Manrique, to examine them.

responsible.name: Spanish friars of the religious orders

defended_by.name: Alonso Manrique
defended_by.role: Inquisitor General, who sympathized with Erasmus

defended_by.name: Emperor Charles V
defended_by.role: Whose court protected him at this time

persecution.outcome: The conference was suspended without a verdict, partly because of an outbreak of plague.

persecution.title: Leaves Basel after the city turns Protestant
persecution.summary: When Basel adopted the Reformation in 1529, its council abolished the Mass and images were destroyed in the churches. Erasmus, unwilling to be seen as approving, moved to Catholic Freiburg im Breisgau.

responsible.name: Basel city council
responsible.role: Abolished the Mass and adopted the Reformation

persecution.outcome: He lived in Freiburg until 1535, then returned to Basel, where he died.

persecution.title: All his works banned by the Index of Pope Paul IV
persecution.summary: Pope Paul IV's Index of Forbidden Books placed Erasmus in its first class of authors, those whose entire works were prohibited.
persecution.outcome: The Index issued after the Council of Trent (1564) softened this, banning some works and allowing others in expurgated form.

excommunication_note: Erasmus was never excommunicated. He died a Catholic priest, and in 1535 the pope had offered to make him a cardinal. After his death, Pope Paul IV's Index (1559) treated him as a forbidden author and banned all his works, which is listed below.

excommunications.reason: Placed among the first-class authors whose complete works were forbidden
excommunications.status: Softened by the Tridentine Index (1564); not a personal excommunication

persecuted_others_note: Erasmus generally urged persuasion and peace rather than force against heretics, and criticized the executions of his day. In replies to his Catholic critics in the late 1520s he conceded that the magistrate might execute heretics who were seditious, which historians read as a hardening or ambivalence. His letters also contain hostile remarks about Jews, such as "if it is Christian to hate Jews, here we are all Christians in abundance", but he did not call for action against them.

persecuted_others.title: Conceded the death penalty for seditious heretics
persecuted_others.summary: Answering censures by Noël Béda and the Paris theology faculty, Erasmus wrote that heretics should first be corrected by teaching, but that the magistrate could put to death those who disturbed public order, much as thieves are punished. He kept insisting that error alone was not grounds for execution, so scholars disagree on how far this changed his earlier stance.

sources.citation: Collected Works of Erasmus, vol. 1: The Correspondence of Erasmus, Letters 1 to 141, trans. R. A. B. Mynors and D. F. S. Thomson (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1974).
Johan Huizinga, Erasmus and the Age of Reformation (1924; New York: Harper Torchbooks, 1957).
Léon-E. Halkin, Erasmus: A Critical Biography, trans. John Tonkin (Oxford: Blackwell, 1993).
